mockText: 100 questions in 2 hours, with flags and a review screen. The real CC is adaptive: 100 to 125 questions, one at a time, and you can't go back. Practice the same way: answer each one and keep moving.
lead: ISC2's entry-level cert, Certified in Cybersecurity. It proves you know the core ideas of security: risk, access control, networks, cloud and incident response. No experience is required, which makes it a strong first cert for anyone new to cyber.

v26.label: 2026 outline
v26.note: ISC2 updated the CC outline on September 1, 2026, with new domain names and more on governance, cloud and threat intelligence. Older books and videos may still follow the previous outline, so make sure their domain names match these.

domains.name: Security Principles
obj: Understand cybersecurity concepts
Confidentiality, integrity, availability, authentication, authorization and accounting (AAA), non-repudiation and privacy.
Understand risk management concepts
The risk management life cycle: identify, assess, treat (avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept) and monitor.
Understand governance concepts
Laws and regulations, frameworks and guidelines, and how policies, standards and procedures fit together.
Understand cybersecurity controls
Technical, administrative and physical controls, and when to use each.
Maintain professional and ethical conduct
Due care and due diligence, codes of conduct and the ISC2 Code of Ethics.

domains.name: Security Governance
obj: Plan governance, risk, and compliance (GRC)
Why GRC matters, and the frameworks and tools organizations use for it.
Understand redundancy
Business continuity (BC) keeps the mission running; disaster recovery (DR) restores the IT.
Understand security awareness
A security culture led from the top, plus training on social engineering, phishing and passwords.
Measure cybersecurity effectiveness
Key metrics and key risk indicators (KRIs), shown on dashboards, scorecards and reports.

domains.name: Identity and Access Management (IAM) Concepts
obj: Understand identity life cycle management
Define roles, then provision, review and deprovision access as people join, move and leave.
Understand logical access controls
Least privilege, separation of duties and access control models (DAC, MAC, RBAC).

domains.name: Networking and Cloud Security Concepts
obj: Understand network security
OSI and TCP/IP models, IPv4 and IPv6, VPNs, firewalls and ports, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, IoT and ICS.
Understand network security architecture
Segmentation (firewall zones, VLANs, microsegmentation), defense in depth and zero trust.
Understand cloud security
Cloud characteristics, service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS), deployment models and the shared responsibility model.

domains.name: Security Operations and Incident Response
obj: Understand data security
Classifying, labeling, masking and sanitizing data, plus symmetric, asymmetric and quantum-resistant encryption and hashing.
Understand security operations
Logging and monitoring, triage and correlation, threat actors and their motives, and threat intelligence.
Understand incident response (IR)
Putting the incident response plan into action, and testing it with exercises such as tabletops.
Understand asset protection
Asset life cycle (including end-of-life gear and software), configuration and change management.
Understand security testing
Red, blue and purple teams, vulnerability scanning, code analysis, threat modeling and physical tests.

extras.title: The core ideas
rows: Only the right people can see the data. Encryption and access control.
The data hasn't been changed without permission. Hashing and signatures.
Systems and data are there when needed. Backups and redundancy.
Who you are, what you may do, and a record of what you did.
You can't deny an action you took. Digital signatures and logs.

extras.title: Ports to know
rows: Remote admin, not encrypted: replace with SSH

extras.title: Cloud: who secures what
rows: You get virtual machines. You patch the OS, apps and data.
The provider runs the OS. You secure your code and data.
The provider runs the app. You manage users, settings and data.
Who has access, and the data itself, are always on you.

extras.title: Incident response, in order
rows: Prepare: a written plan, trained people, tools and contacts.
Detect and analyze: confirm it's really an incident and how bad it is.
Contain: stop the spread, for example by isolating a host.
Eradicate: remove the malware or close the hole.
Recover: restore systems and watch them closely.
Lessons learned: fix the plan so it goes better next time.

method: Use the five domains above as your checklist. Security Principles is the biggest at about a quarter of the exam.
Learn the ideas and the vocabulary. CC tests understanding, not commands or tools.
Tie each idea to your unit: who gets accounts, how backups work, what happens when someone clicks a phishing link.
Flashcards for the CIA triad, control types, risk responses, ports and cloud models.
Timed practice tests, then read every explanation, including the ones you got right.
tips: CC uses computerized adaptive testing (CAT). You answer one question at a time and can't return to earlier ones, so take each one seriously.
The exam stops once it's confident you've passed or failed, anywhere from 100 to 125 questions. Ending early isn't a bad sign.
When answers look close, pick the one that protects people and follows policy, not the quick technical fix.
For ethics questions, protecting society and acting honestly beat doing what a boss or client asks.
Every question needs an answer before you can move on, so make your best pick and keep going.

Exam purchase options, exam windows and attempts.

quiz.q: A finance manager approves a $40,000 payment, then later claims she never approved it. Which control would BEST prove that she did?
o: A digital signature made with her private key
Right. Only she holds her private key, so a valid signature proves the approval came from her. That's non-repudiation.
Encrypting the payment request
Encryption keeps the request secret (confidentiality). It doesn't prove who approved it.
A hash of the payment request
A hash shows the request wasn't changed (integrity), but anyone can make a hash. It doesn't tie the approval to her.
Requiring MFA when she logs in
MFA proves who logged in, but on its own it doesn't create proof that she approved this specific payment.

quiz.q: Securing an old server would cost more than its data is worth, so leadership moves the data and shuts the server down for good. Which risk response is this?
o: Risk avoidance
Right. Stopping the activity that creates the risk removes the risk completely.
Risk transfer
Transfer shifts the cost to someone else, like an insurer or a contractor. Here the risk is simply gone.
Risk mitigation
Mitigation adds controls to reduce the risk while keeping the system. The server was shut down instead.
Risk acceptance
Acceptance means keeping the risk as it is and doing nothing. Leadership acted.

quiz.q: Your supervisor quietly asks you to delete log entries that show a coworker broke policy. According to the ISC2 Code of Ethics, what should you do?
o: Refuse, and report it through the proper channel
Right. The first canons are to protect society and to act honorably and legally. Duty to your employer comes after those.
Delete them, because you must serve your principal
Serving your employer is a canon, but it ranks below protecting society and acting honestly.
Delete them but keep a private copy
That's still destroying evidence, and keeping secret copies isn't honorable conduct either.
Post about it publicly to warn others
Going public skips the proper reporting channels and can harm people unfairly.

quiz.q: A hurricane floods the server room. Which plan covers bringing the IT systems back up at the alternate site?
o: The disaster recovery plan (DRP)
Right. DR is about restoring IT systems and data after a disruption.
The business continuity plan (BCP)
The BCP keeps the whole mission running, with people, places and processes. The IT restore inside it is the DRP's job.
The incident response plan (IRP)
The IRP handles security incidents like malware or breaches, not natural disasters.
The acceptable use policy (AUP)
The AUP sets rules for how people may use systems. It doesn't cover recovery.

quiz.q: Leadership wants an early warning that phishing risk is rising. Which is the BEST key risk indicator (KRI)?
o: The share of people who click in monthly phishing simulations, tracked over time
Right. A KRI signals rising risk before something bad happens. A climbing click rate is exactly that.
The total hours of security training delivered
That measures activity, not risk. People can sit through hours of training and still click.
The number of firewall rules
More rules doesn't say anything about phishing risk.
The number of antivirus licenses purchased
That's an asset count, not an indicator of how likely phishing is to succeed.

quiz.q: A member transfers (PCS) to a new unit. What should happen to their access at the old unit?
o: Remove their old-unit access, then give only what the new role needs
Right. Deprovisioning on transfer prevents privilege creep: access piling up from every job someone has ever had.
Keep everything in case they come back
That's privilege creep. Unneeded access is a risk if the account is ever compromised.
Leave it active for 90 days, then review
Access they no longer need should go when the job changes, not months later.
Add the new access on top of the old
Stacking access is exactly how privilege creep happens.

quiz.q: In the finance system, the same person can add a new vendor AND approve payments to that vendor. Which principle is broken?
o: Separation of duties
Right. Splitting critical steps between two people means one person can't create a fake vendor and pay it.
Least privilege
Least privilege limits access to what a job needs. The specific problem here is one person controlling both halves of a sensitive process.
Need to know
Need to know limits access to information. This is about who can perform which actions.
Defense in depth
Defense in depth means layered controls. It isn't the principle this setup breaks.

quiz.q: Which protocol should replace Telnet for managing a network switch remotely?
o: SSH on port 22
Right. SSH encrypts the whole session, including the password. Telnet sends everything in plain text.
HTTP on port 80
HTTP isn't encrypted either, so it has the same problem as Telnet.
SNMPv1 on port 161
SNMPv1 is for monitoring and sends its community string in plain text.
FTP on port 21
FTP is for moving files, and it isn't encrypted.

quiz.q: Your unit runs a website on virtual machines rented from a cloud provider (IaaS). Who is responsible for patching the operating system on those VMs?
o: Your unit
Right. In IaaS the provider secures the hardware and the hypervisor. The guest OS, apps and data are yours.
The cloud provider
The provider patches what it runs: physical servers, networking and the hypervisor. Not your VM's OS.
Nobody, because the cloud patches itself
Nothing patches itself. Unpatched cloud VMs are a common way in for attackers.
The website's users
Users have no access to the servers.

quiz.q: A smart TV in the break room gets infected. It must not be able to reach the payroll servers. What is the BEST control?
o: Put IoT devices on their own network segment, with firewall rules blocking them from servers
Right. Segmentation limits how far a compromised device can reach. That's defense in depth and zero trust in practice.
Use a longer Wi-Fi password
The TV is already on the network. A stronger password doesn't limit what it can reach.
Install antivirus on the TV
Most smart TVs can't run antivirus, and it wouldn't stop network access anyway.
Turn the TV off at night
It's still reachable, and can still reach others, all day.

quiz.q: A user reports a ransom note on their screen and files they can't open. What should happen FIRST?
o: Disconnect it from the network, leave it powered on, and report it
Right. Containment stops the spread. Leaving it on keeps evidence in memory for the responders.
Turn it off and reimage it
That destroys evidence, and the infection may already have spread. Contain and report first.
Pay the ransom to get the files back
Paying doesn't guarantee recovery and funds criminals. That decision is never the user's to make.
Email the whole unit a screenshot as a warning
Warnings should come from the response team. Containing the machine comes first.

quiz.q: Old hard drives with sensitive data will be reused by another section. Which is the BEST way to prepare them?
o: Sanitize them with an approved wipe (overwrite or cryptographic erase) and verify it
Right. Sanitization makes the old data unrecoverable while keeping the drive usable.
Delete the files and empty the trash
Deleted files can easily be recovered with free tools.
Quick-format the drives
A quick format only resets the file table. The data is still on the disk.
Label the drives as sensitive
Labeling is good practice, but it doesn't remove the data before reuse.

quiz.q: Why are organizations starting to move to quantum-resistant cryptography now, before large quantum computers exist?
o: Attackers can record encrypted data today and decrypt it once quantum computers arrive
Right. This is called 'harvest now, decrypt later'. Secrets that must stay secret for years need protection now.
Current encryption has already been broken
Today's common algorithms are still safe against normal computers.
Hashing will stop working
Quantum computers mostly threaten public-key encryption like RSA. That's the main reason for the switch.
Quantum-resistant algorithms are faster
Speed isn't the reason. Some are actually larger and slower.

pbqs.title: Sort the controls
pbqs.scenario: Your unit's security plan lists these controls. Decide whether each one is technical, administrative or physical. Each type is used twice.

items.log:
Firewall rule blocks inbound Telnet (port 23)
from outside the base network.
items.why: Enforced by technology, so it's a technical (logical) control.

items.log:
Everyone completes security awareness training
before getting a network account.
items.why: Training and policy are administrative (managerial) controls.

items.log:
Badge reader and logbook on the
server room door.
items.why: It controls physical entry, so it's a physical control.

items.log:
Acceptable use policy that every user
signs once a year.
items.why: A written rule people agree to is an administrative control.

items.log:
Multifactor authentication required
for all remote access.
items.why: MFA is enforced by systems, so it's technical.

items.log:
Concrete bollards in front of the
building entrance.
items.why: Bollards stop vehicles physically: a physical control.

pbqs.title: Triage these events
pbqs.scenario: You're on watch in the SOC. For each event, pick the severity and the FIRST action. Each first action is used once.

rows.req: A user mistyped their password once, then logged in normally.
rows.why: Normal behavior. Log it; no action needed unless a pattern appears.

rows.req: A user clicked a phishing link and typed their password into the fake page. No other activity yet.
rows.why: The password is compromised but not yet used. Reset it now (and check for new sign-ins) before an attacker gets in.

rows.req: EDR shows a workstation encrypting files on a shared drive right now.
rows.why: Active ransomware. Isolate the host immediately to stop the damage, then bring in the IR team.

rows.req: An admin account signed in at 03:00 from another country and created three new accounts.
rows.why: A likely compromised admin account with persistence. This needs the incident response team's full process right away.
